title: Modules & Declaration Files
subtitle: import/export with types, type-only imports, .d.ts files, and @types packages
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: TypeScript files import and export code like JavaScript, but types also need to be shared. Without explicit type exports, other files can't use your interfaces, type aliases, or class types across module boundaries.
whyItExists.solution: TypeScript extends JS module syntax with type exports/imports. The import type and export type syntax explicitly marks type-only imports — they're fully erased at compile time (unlike regular imports, which might generate a require() call).
whyItExists.whenToUse: Always. Every non-trivial TypeScript project is module-based. Use import type for types you only need at compile time (interfaces, type aliases, generic parameter types).
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't import type for values that are used at runtime (class instances, enum values, constants). Those need a regular import.

explainModes.beginner: TypeScript can share types between files just like it shares functions and classes. When you only need a type (not actual code) from another file, you can say import type { User } from './user' — TypeScript knows this import exists only to help it check types and erases it completely from the compiled JavaScript.
explainModes.simple: export interface User { ... }. export type ID = string | number. import { User } from './user'. import type { User } from './user' — type-only, erased at compile time. export default class Service { ... }. import Service from './service'. Re-export: export { User } from './user'. Barrel: index.ts that re-exports everything.
explainModes.standard: Declaration files (.d.ts): pure type definitions with no runtime code. They describe the types of JavaScript libraries. @types packages (e.g. npm install -D @types/node) provide .d.ts files for libraries that don't ship TypeScript. allowJs: true — TypeScript can type-check plain JS files. checkJs: true — report errors in JS files. declaration: true in tsconfig — emit .d.ts files alongside your JS output when building a library.
explainModes.technical: import type is erased at emit — it never generates a require() or import statement. This is important for: (1) avoiding circular dependency issues, (2) ensuring no side effects from type-only imports, (3) tools like esbuild that don't run the TypeScript compiler and need to know what to erase. verbatimModuleSyntax (tsconfig option, TS 5.0): forces you to use import type for type-only imports — errors if you use regular import for something that's type-only.
explainModes.deepDive: Module resolution: TypeScript resolves modules using the same algorithm as Node.js by default. moduleResolution: 'bundler' (TS 5.0) for bundler environments that support exports field in package.json. paths in tsconfig for path aliases: paths: { '@/*': ['./src/*'] }. exports field in package.json overrides main for module resolution — TypeScript reads the types field in exports for type declarations. isolatedModules: true forces every file to be a valid module in isolation (required by esbuild/swc which compile file-by-file).

questions.question: What is the advantage of `import type { User }` over `import { User }`?
options: import type is faster at runtime
import type is guaranteed to be erased at compile time — no require() or import statement in the JS output, no side effects
import type allows importing from .d.ts files; regular import does not
They are identical — the type keyword is just documentation
questions.explanation: import type is guaranteed to be erased completely during compilation — it never generates a require() or ES import statement in the output. This matters because: (1) no accidental side effects from the imported module's initialization code, (2) tools like esbuild that compile file-by-file without type information need to know what to drop, (3) some bundlers use this to optimize tree-shaking.

faq.a: When a JavaScript library doesn't ship TypeScript types itself. npm install -D @types/node adds types for Node.js built-ins. @types/react adds React types. Modern libraries (zod, prisma, tanstack query) bundle their own types and don't need a separate @types package. Check the library's README or look for a types or typings field in its package.json.
